334: I've comforted people afraid of turbulence by pretending I have never once thought about it.
335: The job is mostly kindness and balance, delivered sideways, while carrying something hot.
336: I know every word on the safety card. I have watched exactly no one else read a single one.

339: My cart is small, the aisle is smaller, and somehow everyone's elbow still finds it.

348: I have seen a suitcase held together with one hopeful strap and a great deal of optimism.

360: I have sailed to the far corners of the world. I remember them as wet, and quite far away.

379: The sea is my whole career and I still could not tell you what is at the bottom of it.

387: I keep order among a hundred boats. Order among a hundred boats is a generous word for it.
388: My whole world is this one patch of water and its comings and goings. The comings, mostly.
389: I watch the tides all day. They come, they go, they never once ask my opinion.
390: I have the finest view of the water, and I spend most of the day looking down at a clipboard instead.
391: Ships arrive with grand stories. I nod, wave them to a berth, and return to my very still chair.
392: I signal the boats where to go. Where I go is the same office, every day, at the same slow pace.
393: The harbor never sleeps, which is a kind way of saying neither, most nights, do I.
394: I am in charge of everything that floats here. I, personally, would rather not float at all.
395: Every captain thinks their arrival is special. To me it is one more day, with a bit more rope involved.
396: People ask me the fastest way to the sea. I point straight ahead. It is always, reliably, straight ahead.

399: I stay firmly on land while everyone drifts off. Someone has to be here when they all drift back in.
400: I ask everyone the same question all day: anything to declare? Almost everyone says no. Almost everyone is wrong.
401: My whole job is one question. You would think people would practice the answer before they reach my desk.

403: People forget the strangest things. A whole cheese. A second suitcase. Once, a small tree.
404: I ask what you are carrying. The honest ones list three things. The bag, if asked, would list nine.
405: A man told me he had nothing to declare, then his bag began to hum. I still think about that bag.
406: I have heard every version of nothing. Some of them weigh forty pounds.
407: My favorite moment is when a perfectly calm face suddenly remembers the one thing it hoped I would not ask about.
408: You declare nothing. I nod. Then I open the bag and we both learn something new.
409: I spend my days sorting the honest travelers from the optimistic ones. Usually they turn out to be the same traveler.
410: People pack their whole life into a bag, then swear the bag is empty. I admire the confidence.
411: Anything to declare, I ask. They pause. That pause tells me more than any answer ever could.
412: Once a traveler declared a sandwich. Just one sandwich. Honestly, it was refreshing.
413: The job is simple: ask, wait, believe nothing, and smile the whole time anyway.
414: I have watched grown adults forget an entire second coat they were, at that moment, wearing.
415: Every day I learn what people think does not count. It is usually the biggest item in the bag.
416: A woman said no, then produced eleven jars of jam from a coat clearly designed for holding jam.
417: I ask, they answer, and somewhere at their feet a suitcase quietly disagrees with all of it.
418: This job trained me to notice the one bag a person is trying very hard not to look at.
419: People declare the boring things and forget the interesting ones. To be fair, so would I.
420: I lift boxes all day. I do not know what is inside them. I stopped wondering a long time ago.
421: My back has opinions now. It shares them every morning, loudly, before I have even stood up.
422: I carried a crate today that weighed more than I do. We did not part as friends.
423: People ask what I do. I move heavy things from one place to a slightly less convenient place.
424: Every crate looks the same until you lift it. Then it becomes a very personal experience.
425: Once a huge crate turned out to be completely empty. I have never felt more personally betrayed by a box.
426: The dock has one rule: if it is heavy, it belongs to me. Everything here is heavy.
427: I moved forty crates before lunch. Then lunch arrived, and it was also heavy, so I moved that too.
428: You grow strong doing this. You also grow very good at not thinking about your knees.
429: A crate today was marked fragile. It weighed as much as a small horse. I was gentle anyway.
430: My whole life is picking up one heavy thing and setting it down near another heavy thing.
431: I do not ask what is in the boxes. Curiosity has never once helped me lift one.
432: Some days the crates win. You set them down, nod at them, and agree to try again tomorrow.
433: I have strong arms and a short memory. Both are absolutely required for this job.
434: The heaviest crate always sits at the very bottom. I suspect the dock was designed by someone who dislikes me.
435: I stacked boxes taller than my own house. Then someone told me they go on a different boat.
436: People think it is all muscle. It is mostly patience, and a little quiet complaining under my breath.
437: I carried something so heavy today that I briefly forgot my own name. It was a peaceful moment.
438: The crates never say thank you. Years ago, I stopped waiting for them to start.
439: Lift it, carry it, set it down, do it again. My shoulders keep a very detailed record of every single one.
440: My boat is small. The ships are enormous. Somehow I am in charge, and it surprises me daily.
441: I push things a hundred times my size. My little boat has never once complained. I complain plenty.
442: People see a giant ship move and assume it decided to. No. That was me, and my very small boat.
443: The ship weighs more than a mountain. I nudge it politely and hope very much for the best.
444: My entire career is convincing enormous things to move slightly to the left.
445: I have the smallest boat in the harbor and the largest responsibilities in it. It works, mostly.
446: A ship this big has no idea where the harbor entrance is. Luckily, one very small boat knows exactly.
447: I spend my days pushing something that could crush me, very slowly, and with great affection.
448: A ship this size cannot stop quickly. So mostly my job is starting to stop it long before anyone thinks we should.
449: Push too hard and the ship swings the wrong way. So I push almost gently, and apologize quietly when I do not.
450: People wave at the giant ship. Nobody waves at the little boat doing all the work. I wave back anyway.
451: My boat is tiny and stubborn. Between the two of us, the stubborn part does most of the actual work.
452: I once pushed a ship so long that by the time the front reached the dock, the back was still thinking about it.
453: The trick is patience. You cannot rush something that big. Believe me, over the years I have tried.
454: My job is being small and confident next to something huge and helpless. We truly need each other.
455: I spend hours moving a ship a short distance. It is the most important short distance in the harbor.
456: A giant vessel, a tiny boat, and me in the middle, quietly steering the whole disagreement.
457: People underestimate small boats. So do the big ships, right up until the moment I push them.
458: I do not fight the big ships. I lean on them, gently, until they finally agree to go where I want.
459: My boat is little. My determination is not. That, honestly, is the entire job.
460: I know four phrases. I use all four constantly. It has served me beautifully so far.
461: I heard something. I will now repeat it to everyone, forever. This is my job. I adore my job.
462: I want a cracker. I wanted one before you arrived. I will want one long after you leave.
463: I sit on a shoulder and repeat what people say. Nobody tells me secrets anymore. I cannot imagine why.
464: I have strong opinions and one tiny beak. Both of them are extremely loud.
465: The sailors lower their voices whenever I am near. It never helps. My hearing is the best thing about me.
466: I only know a few words, but I say each one at maximum volume. Also, I would like a cracker.
467: People think I do not understand them. I understand plenty. I simply choose to shout it back.
468: I repeat the gossip whether or not it is true. Accuracy was never part of my job description.
469: I have sat on this shoulder for years. I have heard everything. I have kept none of it to myself.
470: Give me a cracker and I will tell you nothing useful, loudly, and with tremendous confidence.
471: I know exactly three things, and I am wrong about one of them. I will not tell you which.
472: The captain keeps telling me to be quiet. The captain does not seem to know who is truly in charge here.
473: I repeat what I hear. If you did not want it repeated, you should not have said it near a bird.
474: I have opinions about the weather, the food, and you specifically. Mostly about the cracker situation.
475: Everyone thinks the parrot is decoration. The parrot heard what you said last night. The parrot remembers.
476: I say the same phrase a hundred times a day. It is a good phrase. Why change something that works.
477: I would tell you a secret, but first, and this part is important, I am going to need a cracker.
478: I am small, I am loud, and I know things. It is a dangerous combination, and I enjoy every part of it.
479: They taught me polite words. I use them to spread gossip. On the whole, a very fair trade.
480: I am not allowed to move a single muscle. The pigeons figured this out weeks ago. They now treat me as furniture.
481: Standing perfectly still is the entire job. You would be amazed how tiring doing nothing can be.
482: I have stood here for hours without moving. My greatest enemy today is one very persistent itch.
483: Visitors pose beside me for photos. I hold the pose far better than they do. It is the one contest I always win.
484: My job is to be a statue that quietly breathes. Most days I forget the breathing part is even allowed.
485: I may not move. I may not speak. Yet here I am, doing both, for you. Please do not tell anyone.
486: People try to make me laugh all day. They fail. But I keep a small private list of the good ones.
487: My greatest professional skill is looking like a man who is not counting the minutes. I am always counting the minutes.
488: The rule is no blinking. I blink. I am, in my own small way, a rebel. Please keep this between us.
489: I stand guard for hours and nothing happens. I guard that nothing with tremendous dedication.
490: Small children salute me all day long. I am not permitted to salute back. That, honestly, is the hardest rule of all.
491: My whole training was learning to do absolutely nothing, flawlessly, for a very long time.
492: A fly landed on my nose this morning. I did not move. That was the highlight of my entire week.
493: I am not supposed to react to anything. So whatever you do, I will stand here and quietly judge it.
494: The uniform is warm and the pose never changes. On long afternoons I am fairly sure I nap standing up, unnoticed.
495: Guides walk past and describe me to strangers as if I cannot hear. I hear all of it. I remember the flattering parts.
496: I stand so still that visitors check whether I am real. I let them wonder. It helps pass the time.
497: My back aches, my feet ache, and I am allowed to show none of it. Being a statue has hidden costs.
498: I am risking a great deal to tell you this: it is very, very boring being this impressive.
499: They chose me to stand here because I never fidget. If they only knew what my mind does all day.
500: My job is to stand very still and look serious. I am extremely good at both.
501: I was told to guard this spot. Nobody said until when, so I assume forever.
502: I follow orders. Today's order was 'wait here.' I have been winning at it all day.
503: I stood so still a bird sat on my helmet. I let it stay. It seemed to have a plan.
504: Guarding is mostly standing. Standing is mostly thinking about sitting.
505: I've been at this post so long I've given all the cracks in the wall names.
506: They gave me a spear and a place to stand. The spear does less than you would think.
507: My commander says patience is a weapon. If so, I am dangerously well armed.
508: I waited four hours for an order. The order was to keep waiting. I respect the consistency.
509: I salute, I stand, I wait. Then, for variety, I stand a little differently.
510: I guarded this gate all morning. A cat walked through. I let it. It outranks me in confidence.
511: Following orders is simple. The hard part is remembering which way I was told to face.
512: I stand watch so nothing happens. So far, a triumph. Nothing keeps not happening.
513: My feet fell asleep at this post. I did not. Someone has to stay alert.
514: I've stared down this road so long I feel like I own it. I do not own it.
515: They spent a year training me to march. I have spent every year since standing perfectly still.
516: Waiting is my whole trade. I have gotten so good I can do it with my eyes half open.
517: A soldier waits. I have waited for orders, for weather, for lunch, and now for this chat.
518: I hold this position no matter what. Nobody has tested it, but I stay ready and slightly bored.
519: I stand guard through rain and sun. Mostly I stand guard through nothing at all.
520: I lean in close and whisper wisdom. Most of it is 'perhaps we should wait and see.'
521: I advise the crown on grave matters. This morning the grave matter was the breakfast menu.
522: I say things slowly and importantly. It makes the smallest suggestion sound enormous.
523: My advice is always the same: proceed with caution. I have built a whole career on it.
524: I whisper into royal ears. Half of what I whisper is simply 'that is a wise question.'
525: A councillor must look thoughtful at all times. I furrow my brow even when I am only hungry.
526: I gave a long, grand speech today. Its point was that we should think about it a while longer.
527: I nod gravely, stroke my chin, and say 'indeed.' That is roughly ninety percent of the job.
528: They pay me to have opinions. I have learned to have them very, very slowly.
529: My counsel is priceless. It is also, if I am honest, mostly 'let us not be hasty.'
530: I stand near the throne and murmur. The murmuring is the important part, apparently.
531: I advised the king to wait until morning before deciding. It is my finest and most frequent advice.
532: I speak in a low, wise voice. Even 'good morning' sounds like a warning when I say it.
533: Grand titles, grand robes, grand whispers. The whispers usually mean 'ask someone else.'
534: I am consulted on everything. My answer to everything is a long, meaningful pause.
535: A councillor never rushes. I have kept the whole court waiting on a single word for an hour.
536: I whisper my advice so no one can steal it. Mostly no one else wants it.
537: I bow deeply and speak wisely. The wisdom, this time, is that we should form a committee.
538: I have advised three kings. Each one, in the end, did the opposite. I remain very proud.
539: My whole role is to look wise and lean in close. The leaning is surprisingly tiring.
540: I watch numbers go up and down all day. Today they went down, then up, then it was lunch.
541: My job is to stare at the numbers until they mean something. I am patient. The numbers are more patient.
542: The numbers rose. Then they fell. I wrote down that they did both. That is the whole report.
543: I study patterns for a living. Today's pattern was that I got hungry at exactly the same time.
544: A number went up. I felt joy. It came back down. I felt informed.
545: I watch the figures so closely that when they blink, I blink too. They do not blink.
546: My conclusion, after hours of careful study, is that the numbers are up. Also that they are down.
547: I turn columns of numbers into meaning. Today the meaning was 'perhaps have a sandwich.'
548: The chart went up sharply. My heart went with it. Then the chart quietly changed its mind.
549: I have looked at these numbers so long I have started to root for a few of them.
550: People ask me what the numbers mean. I tell them, gravely, 'it depends.' They nod as if satisfied.
551: I predicted the numbers would move. They moved. I have never been so unsurprised.
552: My whole trade is watching things rise and fall. Today, mostly, it was my own attention.
553: The figures wobbled all morning. I wrote 'the figures wobbled.' It is a strong report.
554: I sat with these numbers until they confessed. They confessed nothing. They are a very disciplined bunch.
555: I measure everything. This morning I measured how long until I could reasonably stop measuring.
556: The numbers are telling a story. It is a slow story. It is mostly about the numbers.
557: I found meaning in the data at last. It was a very small meaning. I wrote it down anyway.
558: Up, down, up again. I nod at each one as if I expected it. I did not.
559: My job is patience and columns. Today the columns won, and my patience quietly left for lunch.
560: I shout 'buy' and 'sell' all day. Now I shout them at home too, at the soup.
561: My reflexes are stuck from the trading floor. I nearly bought a passing pigeon this morning.
562: I've spent so long yelling numbers that I greeted my own mother with a price.
563: Buy, sell, buy, sell. I do it so fast I sometimes sell things I quite liked.
564: The floor is loud. I am loud. When I go quiet, people ask if something is wrong.
565: I raised my hand to wave hello and accidentally agreed to a very large deal.
566: My hands move faster than my thoughts. Some days I trade before I have fully woken up.
567: I shout all day at the exchange. My voice has two settings now: loud and slightly less loud.
568: I sold, then bought, then sold again, all before breakfast. Breakfast was not for sale.
569: My reflexes never switch off. I flinched at a falling leaf as if it were terrible news.
570: I buy high, sell higher, and shout the whole time. My throat files a complaint every evening.
571: On the floor I never stop moving. At dinner my hand still signals for prices no one is offering.
572: I've shouted 'sold' so often that I once said it when a waiter cleared my plate.
573: Fast hands, loud voice, quick decisions. Choosing what to have for lunch, though, takes me an hour.
574: I trade all day at full speed. When I finally sit still, the whole room feels too slow.
575: Somebody sneezed and my hand shot up to make an offer. Old habits are very fast habits.
576: I yell buy, I yell sell, I yell it with my whole chest. Quiet rooms make me deeply nervous.
577: My reflexes are so trained that I once made a bid at my own reflection. It did not accept.
578: All day it is prices and shouting. By evening I can only whisper, and I still whisper numbers.
579: I make a hundred snap decisions before noon. Then I cannot decide which chair to sit in.
580: I run notes across the whole city on foot. I have met every hill in it, personally.
581: I have the fastest legs in town and, by a wide margin, the sorest feet.
582: I ran three notes across the city before noon. Then I looked around for a fourth, out of pure habit.
583: My job is to run and not read. I have carried a thousand secrets, and kept every one unread.
584: I know every street, every shortcut, every stray dog by name. The dogs, sadly, do not know mine.
585: I delivered a note so fast the sender was still writing the next one when I got back.
586: People say I fly across town. I do not. I run. My feet would like this clearly noted.
587: I've run this city end to end so often I could do it with my eyes closed. I have not tried.
588: My legs never tire. My feet, however, hold a grudge that grows a little bigger each day.
589: I carry messages, not opinions. I once delivered an insult and a love note in one trip, at the same speed.
590: I once raced a rider on a horse across town. I lost. But I looked far more determined about it.
591: I have a perfect memory for doorways and none for faces. I reach the right house and greet the wrong person.
592: I run all day and rest by walking slowly. My idea of a relaxing holiday is a gentle jog.
593: I've worn out more shoes than I can count. The shoes gave up. My legs did not.
594: I delivered forty notes today. I remember every single route and not one single word.
595: They call me the fastest in the city. I have never slowed down enough to see if it is true.
596: I run so much that when I finally sit down, my legs keep going without me for a moment.
597: I've crossed this city so many times I recognize the cobblestones one by one.
598: My whole trade is speed. I am so used to hurrying that now I eat, sleep, and think quickly too.
599: I carried an urgent note across town in record time. It said 'no reply needed.' They always do.
600: I sell hats. Just hats. If you want gossip, that stall is two down and much cheaper.
601: I shout about hats all day. My voice is tired. The hats are fine.
602: People ask if the hats come with a story. No. They come with a brim.
603: I have forty hats and one customer. He is looking at the trinkets.
604: A good hawker sells you a hat you did not know you wanted. I am a good hawker.
605: I called out to a hundred people today. Two waved. One bought a hat.
606: My trinkets are shiny. My hats are practical. I recommend both, loudly.
607: I know every face on this street. I do not know their names. I know their hat size.
608: Someone asked me for a secret. I offered a hat instead. He took the hat.
609: I sell hats, not information. The hats are much better made.
610: By evening I have no voice left, so I sell the last few hats by pointing and looking hopeful.
611: I can spot a head that needs a hat from across the square. It is a quiet talent.
612: A trinket for luck, a hat for the sun. I do not sell luck, honestly.
613: I lowered my voice once, to rest it. Sold nothing. Back to shouting.
614: The best hat I own is on my own head. It is not for sale. Do not ask.
615: Children like the trinkets. Adults pretend not to. Then they buy two.
616: I have described this hat forty times today. It is still just a hat.
617: My stall is loud on purpose. A quiet hat seller is just a man standing near hats.
618: I do not pick my customers. The sun does. On a bright day, everyone suddenly needs a hat.
619: End of the day, I count the hats I have left. That tells me how loud to be tomorrow.
620: I could sell this at the asking price. But then what would we talk about?
621: Every coin matters to me. I once haggled over one for a full hour. I enjoyed it.
622: You offer half, I ask for double, we meet in the middle. That is friendship.
623: I do not lose sleep over the goods. I lose sleep over the last coin of a good haggle.
624: A customer paid my full price today without arguing. I felt cheated, somehow.
625: A quick sale leaves me restless. Make me fight for every coin, or I feel we skipped the good part.
626: My prices are firm. My prices are also flexible. It depends on how you ask.
627: I count my coins twice each night. Once for the total, once for the joy of it.
628: Everything on this stall has two prices. The one I say, and the one you earn.
629: You want a discount? Sit down. This will take a while, and I have tea.
630: I have argued over the price of a button. I regret nothing. I won the button.
631: A fair deal is one where we both walk away sure we cheated the other.
632: I never name my lowest price first. That would end the conversation too soon.
633: Some sell to be rich. I sell to argue. The coins are just how we keep score.
634: You will pay more than you wanted and less than I hoped. That is a good market.
635: I remember every haggle I have ever lost. There are two. I still think about them.
636: My grandmother taught me to haggle. She once argued with the tax man, and won.
637: The goods change every week. The bargaining does not. That is the real business.
638: I raised my price when you frowned, because a frown means you still want it.
639: Come back tomorrow and we will do this all again. I look forward to it, truly.
640: Grown-ups walk right past me. So I see everything they do when they think no one is.
641: Nobody watches a kid. That is why a kid sees the most. Also, do you have any bread?
642: I know which stalls watch me closely and which do not. I remember the ones that do not.
643: Adults think I am not listening. So they say the interesting things right in front of me.
644: I counted forty people cross this square today. I counted their pockets too. Old habit.
645: You want to know who came by? Ask the kid nobody looked at twice.
646: I remember every face that has ever shooed me off this corner. It is a long list.
647: Nobody tells me anything, so I just watch. Watching is free. Food, sadly, is not.
648: I saw the whole thing. Grown-ups never think to ask the small one in the corner.
649: I know every shortcut in this city. The grown-ups take the long way and call it dignity.
650: People whisper near me like I am furniture. I hear it all. I forget none of it.
651: I have stood on this corner so long the pigeons treat me as one of their own.
652: A kid on the street is invisible. Very handy. Less handy at dinnertime.
653: I notice when a stranger looks nervous. I also notice when a baker looks away.

2802: Butterflies taste with their feet. Every landing is also a small snack decision.
2803: Cats cannot taste sweetness at all. They simply do not see the appeal.
2804: Elephants cannot jump. All four feet simply stay on the ground, and they seem entirely at peace with it.
2805: Owls can turn their heads about three-quarters of the way around, so they never bother turning the body.
2806: Hummingbirds are the only birds that can fly backwards. They leave a room whenever they like.
2807: A giraffe has exactly seven bones in its neck, the same as you. Theirs are just longer.
2808: Camels store fat in their humps, not water. A mix-up they have never bothered to correct.
2809: Polar bears have black skin under all that white fur. A rather well-kept secret.
2810: Reindeer eyes turn from gold in summer to blue in winter. Even their eyes notice the cold.
2811: Goats have rectangular pupils and can see nearly all the way around. Very little sneaks up on a goat.
2812: Koalas sleep up to twenty hours a day. The other four hours are also fairly restful.
2813: Sloths can hold their breath longer than dolphins by slowing their heart right down. Unhurried, as ever.
2814: Starfish have no brain and no blood, and get along perfectly well anyway.
2815: A snail carries thousands of tiny teeth. It is in no hurry to use them.
2816: Some frogs freeze almost solid in winter, then thaw out in spring and hop away, good as new.
2817: Axolotls can regrow a lost limb, and even parts of the heart. Very tidy of them.
2818: Bees can learn to recognize human faces. You may already have been noticed.
2819: Honeybees give directions by dancing. A little wiggle means lunch is that way.
2820: Penguins of some kinds propose with one carefully chosen pebble. Romance, essentially.
2821: Dolphins invent a personal whistle and use it as a name. Everyone gets one, ready or not.
2822: Flamingos are born grey and turn pink from the shrimp they eat. The color is a diet choice, really.
2823: A blue whale's tongue alone can weigh as much as an elephant. The rest of the whale is also large.
2824: Ostriches have eyes larger than their brains. They do see wonderfully, at least.
2825: A chameleon's tongue can be longer than the rest of it. Reach is not the problem.
2826: Kangaroos cannot easily walk backwards. They committed to forward long ago.
2827: A flea can jump many times its own height. Small, and fully aware of it.
2828: Some turtles live well past a hundred years, in no particular hurry to stop.
2829: Bananas are, botanically, berries. Strawberries technically are not. Nobody asked us.
2830: Peanuts are not nuts at all, but grow underground like beans. A quiet identity matter.
2831: Cashews grow dangling from the bottom of a soft, apple-like fruit, like an afterthought.
2832: A single pineapple can take nearly two years to grow. Worth the wait, it insists.
2833: Chocolate begins as seeds inside a fruit that grows on a tree. Good news, arguably.
2834: Watermelon is roughly nine parts water out of ten. Refreshing, and honest about it.
2835: Mushrooms are more closely related to animals than to plants. A quiet family surprise.
2836: Bamboo can grow almost a meter taller in a single day. Impatient, for a plant.
2837: Young sunflowers turn through the day to follow the sun. Older ones give up and just face east.
2838: The Sun holds nearly all the mass in the whole solar system. The rest of us are a rounding error.
2839: A day on Venus lasts longer than a whole year there. Time behaves oddly over there.
2840: Footprints left on the Moon may stay put for millions of years. No wind to tidy them away.
2841: A single cloud can weigh hundreds of tons, yet floats along completely untroubled.
2842: That fresh smell after rain comes from tiny bacteria in the soil. They deserve the credit.
2843: A spoonful of a collapsed star would weigh billions of tons. Best left where it is.
2844: There are more stars in the universe than grains of sand on every beach on Earth. A generous amount.
2845: An ant can carry many times its own weight without complaint. Or with very silent complaint.
2846: Tomatoes are, botanically, a fruit. They keep this to themselves at dinner.
